title: The logistics of building a weight lifting platform to save money
summary: NH covers the planning and logistics of building a home gym lifting platform (his is 16x8 ft and saved him about $3,000). He covers chalk-marking the space, writing a step-by-step plan, buying high-quality plywood in person, using horse stall mats, doing a mock assembly, and screwing rather than gluing the top layer so worn pieces can be replaced.

claims.claim: Building a platform yourself instead of buying retail saved him about $3,000.
A platform protects the floor by combining a rigid wood structure with mats; a small 2x4 deadlift platform can be moved, but his 16x8 ft one can't.
Mark the footprint on the floor with chalk, measure it, and write every detail down so you don't freeze at the hardware store.
Decide how much protection you need: one layer of plywood plus mat over solid ground, or two layers of plywood for more; more layers cost more and are harder to move.
If you'll bolt a rack to the platform, plan where the screws go and buy wood/mat screws, since racks usually come with concrete anchors.
Draw a step-by-step paper plan (layers, piece counts, dimensions, cuts, screws, glue) a month or two before buying materials; get wood cut at the store if you lack tools.
Don't use cheap plywood underneath: it's often warped and makes a wobbly surface for deadlifts. Quality plywood costs about three times more but lasts years.
Never buy plywood online; stores offload the worst stock. Inspect every sheet in person for warping and knots, which make screwing impossible.
The exposed top wood piece takes the most abuse (humidity, sweat, impact), so buy the best quality you can for it.
Buy high-quality horse stall mats, not puzzle-piece mats from websites.
Rent a truck and bring at least one strong helper to haul plywood and mats.
Do a full mock assembly before gluing or screwing, so you can fix the plan if it doesn't match.
Garage floors slope, so you need to calculate a structure that levels the platform.
Glue the base layers before screwing and let the glue dry first; in warm weather his dried in about 40 minutes.
Don't glue the mats or the exposed top wood; screw them only, so a cracked or worn piece can be swapped for about $30 instead of rebuilding the platform.
He once cracked the exposed wood by dropping a weight during squats.
A large multi-layer platform becomes immovable as a unit; removing it means unscrewing every piece.
